Deck overview
Read a record without revealing which one

A database server holds bits . The client wants bit , but wants to hide the index from the server. This is private information retrieval, or PIR. The index identifies the requested record; the database's contents are not assumed secret from the client.

For a DNS-style lookup, learning which record is requested can reveal which service the client intends to use. Encrypting the network connection protects against an outside eavesdropper, but the answering server still sees an ordinary query. PIR addresses that server-side visibility.

Downloading all bits and choosing locally solves the privacy problem. The challenge is to communicate less than the whole database. We will follow two routes: split the query between non-colluding servers, or encrypt it for one server. These protocols retrieve an indexed item; converting an arbitrary search phrase into a suitable private database query is an additional problem.

‹
Separate correctness, privacy and cost

A two-server protocol has three stages: produces queries ; each server runs ; the client reconstructs its bit from the answers and retained local information. The subscript labels a server.

RequirementWhat to check
CorrectnessWhen the parties follow the protocol, reconstruction returns Xᵢ.
Query privacyOne server cannot distinguish which allowed index was requested from its view.
CommunicationCount both uploaded queries and downloaded answers, in bits.

Sublinear means the communication divided by tends to zero as grows. This is written . For example, tends to zero, but does not. The notation is an upper growth bound, not an exact bit count.

Privacy does not promise correct answers from malicious servers, conceal the fact that a query happened, or limit the client to learning one record. Those are separate guarantees. In particular, the lecture's non-collusion condition concerns query privacy; a server that deliberately changes its answer can still spoil reconstruction.

An index can be represented by a vector

A vector is an ordered list. The one-hot vector has a 1 at position and 0 everywhere else. For four positions, .

For now, arithmetic is in . Addition keeps the remainder modulo 2: it is XOR, written . Thus . Multiplication of bits is AND: only gives 1.

Read this inner product as “multiply corresponding entries, then XOR the products”. A query bit 1 includes a database bit in that XOR; a query bit 0 excludes it. Consequently .

Sending directly would reveal the index. We need to hide this vector while preserving a way to compute its inner product.

Hide the selector in two individually random shares

Choose a uniform random bit vector , meaning all vectors are equally likely. Define , with XOR applied at each position. The pair satisfies , since XORing any bit with itself cancels it.

This is additive secret sharing over . Each server receives one share. For any fixed selector, XOR with it rearranges all possible random masks. Thus either share alone has the same uniform distribution for every index.

Non-collusion means the servers do not pool their views. If they do, combining the shares reveals the selector. For repeated queries, use a fresh random mask each time; reusing one mask would create relations between the observed queries.

The first private protocol: XOR the two answers

Both servers hold the same database . Server returns the single bit . The client XORs the replies. Distributing the inner product over XOR gives

Every random mask cancels, so honest reconstruction is always correct. Privacy follows from the single-share distributions established on the previous card; the answer is just a function of the server's database and that share.

Count the cost carefully: the client uploads two -bit vectors and downloads two bits, for bits total. Hiding the index worked, but we have not achieved sublinear communication.

If each record instead contains bits, apply the same selector to every bit position within a record. Upload remains bits and the two answers contain bits. This observation motivates arranging a bit database into fewer, longer records next.

Reshape the database into rows and columns

Place the database bits into an -row, -column matrix, with . Pad unused cells with known zeros. A matrix is simply a rectangular table; the entry has row and column .

To request , privately select its column. Use -bit shares of . Each server computes , meaning one inner product per row, and returns an -bit vector. Combining the answers reveals the whole column; the client reads row locally.

The row number is never transmitted in this protocol. Changing the row while retaining the column changes only the client's final local selection. Ordinary PIR allows the client to learn the other bits in the reconstructed column.

Why the reshaped protocol still works

Now each have entries and each have . The same cancellation works simultaneously in every row:

The notation means “all rows in column j”. Taking entry of this vector yields , the desired bit. Each equality uses distributivity or cancellation over .

For privacy, each individual query is uniform among all -bit strings, regardless of . The query also contains no row index. Thus the view of either non-colluding server is independent of both coordinates. This proves information-theoretic query privacy, rather than relying on an attacker being unable to solve a difficult computation.

Balance uploads against downloads

The two queries cost bits and the two replies cost bits. With , the total is

Making more columns lengthens queries but shortens replies. The smallest sum occurs at : from , we get , so .

For nonsquare , choose and ; the ceiling symbol means round up to an integer. Padding preserves the bound. Growth rates do not guarantee a saving on tiny inputs: only when .

Which assumption pays for privacy?

Two-server PIR relies on separation of the servers' views. Its uniform-share proof survives even unlimited computation, but not collusion. Single-server PIR cannot obtain sublinear communication with information-theoretic privacy in the standard setting of the lecture; it needs computational assumptions.

RouteWhat privacy relies on
Two replicated serversEach server sees only its own share.
One serverThe server cannot efficiently distinguish encrypted queries.

For the homework's hypothetical world, recall the complexity classes: P contains yes/no questions decidable in polynomial time, while NP contains questions with proposed yes-witnesses checkable in polynomial time. For instance, a proposed key can be checked against a list of function inputs and outputs.

Assuming would collapse the distinction between efficient verification of such a witness and efficient decision of its existence. It would defeat the hardness needed by the cryptographic route. It would not change the fact that two distributions are mathematically identical. Apply that distinction to the two-server scheme now.

HW4 1c · Two servers need a separation assumption

Assume . Can secure two-server PIR with sublinear communication still exist?

Show step-by-step solution

  1. The two servers hold identical copies of the database but do not share their query views. For a matrix with columns, choose a uniform bit vector , and set , where has a 1 only in the requested column.

  2. For every target , each individual share is uniform among the bit vectors. To see this for server 1's share , fix any possible value . Exactly one mask, , produces it. Thus , independently of . Unlimited computation cannot distinguish identical distributions.

  3. With roughly rows and columns, two queries and two answers use bits. Therefore the answer is true: privacy is information-theoretic, conditional on non-collusion. If the servers combine their queries, reveals the column. Correct output still assumes honest answering; privacy alone does not prevent a server from returning a wrong answer.

Compute on an encryption without decrypting it

An encryption algorithm turns a plaintext into a ciphertext , using public key and fresh randomness . Only the client holds the decryption key . Fresh randomness prevents identifying a secret bit by comparing it with one fixed encryption of 0 or 1.

Linearly homomorphic encryption (LHE) lets the server combine ciphertexts so that decryption gives a sum of plaintexts, and multiply a plaintext by a known scalar. Write for encrypted addition and for multiplication by known scalar . Then

These operations use the encryption scheme's plaintext arithmetic. The equalities concern decrypted values; evaluated ciphertext bytes need not equal a fresh encryption's bytes. The server does not learn the plaintext sum.

LHE does not generally multiply two unknown encrypted plaintexts. Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), used later, supports evaluation of whole circuits including such multiplications. Both need an appropriate encryption-security assumption to hide the inputs.

Encrypt the column selector for one server

The client encrypts every component of , using fresh encryption randomness, and sends the ciphertexts. For each row , the server forms an encrypted linear combination using its known database bits as scalars:

The large means combine all these terms with encrypted addition. Since only position of the plaintext selector is 1, decrypting gives . The server returns one ciphertext per row; the client decrypts its desired row.

Upload and download total ciphertexts. If each has bits, communication is , or under the lecture's simplification and square layout. Here is the security parameter. Public setup/key material is accounted for separately when reused.

The encrypted query vectors for different indices must be computationally indistinguishable: efficient tests should not identify which was sent. This is a guarantee about the joint encrypted vector, not about whether one displayed ciphertext looks random.

HW4 1b · Single-server PIR when P equals NP

Assume , without a random oracle. Do secure single-server PIR schemes with sublinear communication exist in the setting of this course?

Show step-by-step solution

  1. Private information retrieval (PIR) hides the requested index from the server. “Sublinear communication” means the number of transmitted bits grows more slowly than database size ; downloading the entire database is excluded from the question.

  2. For a single server, information-theoretic query privacy cannot provide this saving in the standard PIR setting. The single-server constructions in the lecture instead use cryptographic encryption: the server can compute on the query but cannot efficiently identify its plaintext.

  3. The intended answer is false. The computational hardness needed for nontrivial single-server PIR does not survive . Merely possessing encryption algorithms would not suffice; their privacy assumption must remain secure. The whole-database download remains private, but has linear communication.

Retrieve privately from the intermediate answer too

The matrix scheme returns a whole encrypted column even though the client needs one entry. Recursion applies private selection again to that intermediate data. For a simple example, let and label a target by three coordinates , each from 1 to .

Arrange the original database in rows and columns. Selecting column produces inner ciphertexts, indexed by . Reshape them as an -by- table and privately select column . The client receives outer-encrypted records and locally chooses row .

Why can LHE handle the second layer? The server treats the encoding of an inner ciphertext as known data to select, just as it previously treated a database bit as known data. It encrypts that representation under the outer selection; it is not multiplying two hidden plaintexts. Ciphertext encodings may need suitable plaintext blocks. The client removes the outer layer to obtain an inner ciphertext, then decrypts that ciphertext.

Count the size of an encrypted record, not only its number

In the two-selection example, queries contain two length- selector vectors, and the reply contains outer-encrypted records. This suggests objects. It is not yet an -bit claim, because an outer object contains an encoded inner ciphertext.

Let be the number of bits representing an object after encryption layers. If every layer doubles the length, then . A useful low-expansion scheme can have much milder growth; the illustration compares that with an additive-overhead model .

The lecture's polylogarithmic-communication result uses suitable low-expansion linearly homomorphic encryption and the full recursive encoding. “Polylogarithmic” means bounded by a fixed power of , with security-parameter factors retained. It does not follow for an arbitrary LHE scheme merely by repeating selection and ignoring ciphertext lengths.

Why the same recursion cannot simply reuse two-server PIR

The two-server primitive assumed both servers hold the same database. After a private matrix query, server 0 has computed , while server 1 has computed . These are different shares of the selected column, not two copies of that column.

Try the lecture question: what goes wrong?

Calling the same replicated-database PIR protocol on these intermediate answers would violate its input assumption. Giving both answers to a server could expose the reconstructed column and hence information about the target. The single-server encrypted scheme instead leaves the server with a complete table of encrypted intermediate records that it can select from again.

This explains why the naive reuse fails; it is not an impossibility theorem against all more sophisticated multi-server PIR constructions.

Before FHE: describe an address and a Boolean circuit

A one-hot vector for records needs bits. A binary address needs only bits. For eight records, use 000 through 111. We keep record numbers 1 through 8 for reading, and encode record number minus one as its address.

A Boolean circuit connects gates with bit-valued wires. NOT flips a bit, AND outputs 1 only if both inputs are 1, and OR outputs 1 if at least one input is 1.

To select by an encrypted binary address, the server will need to test equality with each record's public address. Start with the ordinary, unencrypted equality circuit in the next exercise. Build the one-bit test from its two accepting cases, then require it to hold at every position.

Turn a binary address into selection bits inside a circuit

For each record , compare its public address with the requested address . Call the equality result . Exactly one is 1 for a valid request. Combine these selectors with the database:

The large means OR all terms. Each unwanted record is masked to 0; the desired record contributes its own bit. OR is appropriate here because at most one selector is 1. It should not be read as ordinary integer addition in general.

FHE evaluates this Boolean circuit on encrypted inputs without revealing its intermediate bits. Unlike LHE, it supports AND between values whose plaintexts are both hidden. For the homework's secret-key scheme, the server also needs encrypted constants supplied by the client; it does not receive the key.

Compactness is the guarantee that the final ciphertext does not grow with the entire evaluated circuit. Parameter choices must also support the circuit's computation correctly. These are the properties needed to make the next exercise's “one returned ciphertext” useful.

HW4 4b · Use an encrypted binary address

Using a secret-key fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) scheme for Boolean circuits, construct one-round single-server PIR on a database of bits with uploaded ciphertexts and one returned ciphertext.

Show step-by-step solution

  1. Use address bits. Number records 1 through , but encode record by the binary representation of , padded to bits. For example, eight records use addresses 000 through 111; trying to encode record 8 as the number 8 would incorrectly need four bits.

  2. The client encrypts its address bits with fresh encryption randomness, and also sends encryptions of 0 and 1. It keeps the secret key. These constants let the server represent each public address and database bit as ciphertext inputs even though it cannot run secret-key encryption itself. Supply any needed query-independent public evaluation material separately.

  3. For each record , the server homomorphically evaluates the equality circuit between the encrypted address and the constant address . The result encrypts a selection bit : 1 for the requested record and 0 for all others. It then computes an encrypted AND of with the database bit , represented by the supplied encrypted constant.

  4. OR the masked results together and return that one ciphertext. Exactly one selector is 1 for a valid address, so all other terms are 0 and the plaintext result is . The client decrypts it. FHE correctness must hold for this entire circuit and the chosen parameters.

  5. Upload is ciphertexts; download is one. Compactness means evaluation does not make the final ciphertext length grow with the entire evaluated circuit. Query privacy follows from the encryption scheme's security for the joint collection of encrypted bits. It is computational privacy, and the server still evaluates a database-wide circuit—short communication is not sublinear server work.

Track the quantity that a gate changes

Many homomorphic schemes carry an error quantity often called noise. Decryption works only while the error stays within the scheme's permitted range. For HW4 we use its stated numerical rules, rather than deriving a particular cryptosystem's error analysis.

Work from input wires toward output wires and label each intermediate result. These magnitudes are not the encrypted bits themselves: a plaintext AND result of 0 does not imply noise 0.

To simplify the final count, remember when is a power of two. Thus . For other database sizes, retain . The next exercise follows the actual gates built in 4(a–b), including their encrypted constants.

  2. AND the equality results for all address positions. Multiplication of their noise magnitudes gives . If is a power of two, , so .

    For power-of-two , this simplifies to the sheet's .

  4. This is a bookkeeping model for this circuit, not a universal noise law for every FHE scheme. Simplifying gates against public constants or using an additional procedure to reduce noise would change the calculation. No decryption threshold is supplied, so the magnitude alone cannot tell us whether a particular cryptosystem's parameters are sufficient.

A short query can still require a full database scan

The constructions above reduce communication while leaving substantial server work. A matrix answer uses the entire table in its row-wise combinations. The FHE construction compares the address with every record and combines every result. With the unsimplified equality circuit, its Boolean gate count is , before the cost of homomorphic gate evaluation.

Why not read only the requested entry? That memory access would reveal the index to the server. For an arbitrary unprocessed database, an algorithm that never examines a particular bit cannot in general return it correctly for both possible values. This is the intuition behind the linear-work obstacle in the basic model.

That intuition is not a lower bound for every possible PIR model. Preprocessing can store derived information, and batching can share work across requests. Those change what “work for this query” means.

Move or share work without pretending it disappears

Batching answers several queries together so they can share database processing. The notes cite a bound of work for a batch of queries. This describes a specialized construction; simply running the original protocol times still costs about scans.

Preprocessing performs work before the individual queries arrive. The offline phase prepares a data structure; the online phase answers each later request. To compare schemes, count the setup once and the online cost once per query. An amortized cost divides that total by the number of served queries.

The notes describe a two-server result with linear offline preprocessing and roughly online communication/work, and a later single-server theoretical result with near-linear encoding and polylogarithmic online complexity. These are separate constructions with their own assumptions, not automatic upgrades to the simple protocols we derived. The next sequence revisits polynomial proofs and commitments because HW4 also tests those midterm topics.

Midterm bridge: prove claims about polynomials

PIR hides a requested index. The remaining HW4 questions return to a different task from Chapter 3: verifying a claim about a polynomial. We now prepare that algebra explicitly, before working through the proof constructions.

Over a prime field , calculate modulo prime . Every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse, so it can be cancelled. A polynomial has coefficients ; its degree is the largest index of a nonzero coefficient. A root is an input for which .

A nonzero degree- polynomial has at most distinct roots over a field. The reason is that a root gives a factor . Any different root must belong to the remaining factor, since can be cancelled. Each new root therefore consumes another degree.

The zero polynomial, whose coefficients are all zero, is the exception: it is zero everywhere. Also, arithmetic modulo a composite number need not permit cancellation. Use the earlier homework question next to check that condition before using the theorem.

  2. Modulo 6, even though neither factor is zero. Thus is not a field; we cannot cancel a nonzero factor as the root-bound proof requires.

    The roots are . There are four of them, so the claim is false.

A degree bound turns a random check into evidence

Fix two polynomials of degree at most before choosing a uniform random field point . If the polynomials differ, their difference is nonzero and has at most roots. Thus checking equality at misses a false identity with probability at most , capped at 1.

HW4 supplies an ideal polynomial oracle: once a polynomial and degree bound are fixed, every query returns an evaluation of that same bounded-degree polynomial. Without that promise, a prover could invent a convenient value after seeing . A large field compared with makes the error small; the two-element field used in bit PIR would generally be too small for this test.

Each coefficient moves up by exactly positions. No term below position remains. This will let the prover express “these low coefficients are zero” as an identity that the verifier can test.

Give the target coefficient a position nobody else can occupy

To certify one coefficient, reserve its degree position and constrain the remaining pieces to lie on either side. The indices count powers, starting with the constant term at position 0.

The next exercise asks you to specify those side polynomials, their degree bounds and the random evaluation check. For an endpoint coefficient, one side is empty and is represented by the zero polynomial.

Midterm check: identify the guarantee and the model

The preceding tests work because a false polynomial identity has few roots. That conclusion holds even against unlimited computation, as long as the polynomials were fixed with the enforced degree limits. Cryptographic commitments are a separate mechanism for implementing that ideal interface.

PropertyMeaning
CompletenessHonest proofs of true claims pass.
SoundnessFalse claims pass only with bounded probability.
KnowledgeA sufficiently successful prover permits extraction of a valid witness.
Zero knowledgeThe verifier's view can be simulated without the witness.

A relation says that witness establishes public statement . Knowledge error is the success threshold above which an efficient extractor must recover such a witness, using its prescribed interaction with the prover. A false statement has no valid witness to extract.

First use HW3 1(a) to distinguish knowledge from soundness. Then apply the separation between ideal oracles and computational implementations to HW4 1(a). Neither exercise claims that every sound proof automatically hides its witness.

HW3 1a · Knowledge implies soundness

An interactive proof has soundness error greater than : some prover convinces the verifier of a false statement with probability greater than . Can it have knowledge error less than ? Explain your answer.

Show step-by-step solution

  1. Soundness concerns false statements. If the public statement is false, there is no witness satisfying the relation .

  2. Knowledge error is the acceptance threshold above which the proof-of-knowledge guarantee requires an efficient extractor to recover a valid witness from the prover. The extractor may interact with and rewind that prover; it does not simply read the transcript.

  3. The cheating prover in the question succeeds with probability greater than . If , that success would trigger extraction on a false statement. This is impossible because no valid witness exists. Thus the sheet’s claim that such a knowledge error is impossible is true.

HW4 1a · An ideal oracle and its cryptographic implementation

Assume in the standard model, without a random oracle. Is the PLONK polynomial IOP still sound?

Show step-by-step solution

  1. A polynomial interactive oracle proof (Poly-IOP) gives the verifier an ideal interface to fixed polynomials with enforced degree bounds. Soundness means a false claim is accepted only with the stated small probability; it does not mean the prover's witness is hidden.

  2. Its algebraic tests choose random points after the relevant polynomials have been fixed. A false degree-bounded identity can hold at only a bounded number of field points. This root-counting fact does not depend on the prover's computing time.

  3. Thus the intended answer is true for the ideal Poly-IOP, including its required consistency checks. The hypothesis does not invalidate a field theorem. It can, however, invalidate the computational commitments used to implement those oracles. Soundness of the ideal object must be distinguished from security of a deployed SNARG.

Midterm check: proof length and verifier time are different

A SNARG is a succinct non-interactive argument. The lecture asks for a short proof and fast verification, allowing the verifier to read the public input:

Vertical bars mean the bit length of a string. The notation “poly” allows fixed powers of its arguments. The bound is more specific than “some polynomial in the statement length”. A cubic-time decider is efficient in the complexity-class sense, but is not thereby a nearly linear-time verifier.

If , an NP statement can be decided without a prover's message. That supplies an empty proof. Before calling it a SNARG under this definition, ask how much work the verifier's decision algorithm performs. This is the distinction the next conceptual question is testing.

HW4 1d · An empty proof is not automatically fast verification

Assume . Does this alone establish that all NP languages have a SNARG under the lecture's succinct-verification requirement?

Show step-by-step solution

  1. P contains decision problems solvable in polynomial time; NP contains problems with efficiently checkable witnesses. If , the verifier can decide an NP statement without receiving a witness. An empty proof therefore gives perfect completeness and soundness.

  2. That establishes short communication. The lecture also asks for verification time , where is the public statement, the witness and the security parameter. Reading the input is allowed, but a general polynomial-time decision algorithm may take much longer.

  3. For example, a running time of is polynomial, yet the assertion “polynomial time” supplies no nearly linear bound in . Thus the intended answer is false in the sense that the conclusion does not follow from this argument. The supplied solution's “unlikely” qualification is not an unconditional impossibility proof. If “succinct” meant only a short proof, the empty-proof observation would answer a different, weaker question.

Public powers let us encode a polynomial evaluation

A group of prime order contains elements. A generator reaches them all as . Group multiplication adds exponents; raising a group element to a known scalar multiplies its exponent:

Exponents are calculated modulo . The identity element is , and a negative exponent means a group inverse. Finding from is the discrete-logarithm problem. An efficiently computable group operation does not imply this inverse problem is easy.

The setup in HW4 chooses a hidden nonzero field element and publishes

Each item is a group element, not the exponent written above it. The prover knows its polynomial coefficients and can use the two power rules to combine these items. Parts 3(a–b) ask what this allows it to compute, and what security can—and cannot—follow from that encoding.

HW4 3b · Why the binding guarantee is computational

Is the commitment statistically or computationally binding? Explain the role of the hidden setup exponent.

Show step-by-step solution

  1. Binding prevents the prover from using different polynomials as explanations of the same commitment. Statistical binding must hold even against an unlimited attacker. Computational binding restricts the attacker to efficient algorithms.

  2. For degree limit , an unlimited attacker can recover from by enumerating discrete logarithms. For any nonzero field scalar , set . This changes the polynomial while preserving , so the commitments agree.

  3. Therefore the scheme is not statistically binding for . The intended guarantee is computational binding under the appropriate polynomial-commitment hardness assumptions for the chosen group and setup. “Many collisions exist” does not prove they are hard to find, and unknown alone is not a proof of that assumption.

  4. The boundary case commits only to constants: the map is one-to-one modulo , so this particular collision argument does not apply. Also, binding does not assert hiding; the deterministic commitment is not automatically a private encoding of the polynomial.
